title: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: The number of molecules in $11.2\ \text{L}$ of a gas at STP is:
questions.solution:
At STP one mole of any gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$.

$n = \dfrac{11.2}{22.4} = 0.5\ \text{mol}$

Number of molecules $= 0.5 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = \mathbf{3.011\times10^{23}}$.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: The maximum number of electrons in a subshell with azimuthal quantum number $l$ is:
questions.solution:
A subshell of given $l$ has $(2l+1)$ orbitals (the values of $m_l$ from $-l$ to $+l$), and each orbital holds **two** electrons of opposite spin.

Maximum $= \mathbf{2(2l+1)}$.

So $s$ ($l=0$) holds 2, $p$ ($l=1$) holds 6, $d$ ($l=2$) holds 10 and $f$ ($l=3$) holds 14.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.solution:
Chromium is one of the two famous exceptions to the filling order.

$\mathbf{[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}}$, not $3d^{4}4s^{2}$, because a **half-filled** $d$ subshell is unusually stable — the exchange energy gained outweighs the cost of promoting the $4s$ electron.

Copper is the other: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}$, for the same reason with a completely filled subshell.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: A compound contains $40\%$ C, $6.7\%$ H and $53.3\%$ O by mass. Its empirical formula is:
questions.solution:
Divide each percentage by the atomic mass to get moles in $100\ \text{g}$:

C: $\dfrac{40}{12} = 3.33$

H: $\dfrac{6.7}{1} = 6.7$

O: $\dfrac{53.3}{16} = 3.33$

Divide through by the smallest ($3.33$):

C : H : O $= 1 : 2 : 1$

Empirical formula $\mathbf{\text{CH}_2\text{O}}$ — which is glucose's empirical formula, its molecular formula being $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers is **not** possible?
questions.solution:
The rule is $l = 0, 1, \ldots, (n-1)$ — so $l$ must be **less than** $n$.

For $n = 2$, $l$ can only be $0$ or $1$. **$n=2, l=2$ is impossible**; there is no $2d$ subshell.

The others are all legal: $m_l$ runs from $-l$ to $+l$ in each case.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: In the reaction $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3$, $1\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{N}_2$ reacts with $2\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$. The limiting reagent is:
questions.solution:
The equation needs $3\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$ per mole of $\text{N}_2$.

Only $2\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$ is supplied, which is enough for just $\dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{N}_2$.

So **$\text{H}_2$ runs out first** and is the limiting reagent; $\dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{N}_2$ is left over.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that:
questions.solution:
$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$.

Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly — not because our instruments are poor, but because a particle does not simultaneously possess both to arbitrary precision.

This is why Bohr's definite orbits had to give way to **orbitals**, which are regions of probability.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: Molality is defined as moles of solute per:
questions.solution:
Molality $= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kilogram of \textbf{solvent}}}$.

Molarity uses litres of **solution** instead. The distinction matters because volume changes with temperature while mass does not — so molality is **temperature-independent**, which is why colligative-property work uses it.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that:
options: Electrons fill the lowest orbital first
Orbitals of equal energy are singly occupied before any is doubled
No two electrons have the same four quantum numbers
questions.solution:
Hund's rule: within a set of **degenerate** orbitals, every orbital is singly occupied, all with parallel spins, before any is doubly occupied.

Pairing two electrons in one orbital costs repulsion energy, so the atom avoids it while empty orbitals of the same energy remain.

The other options are the Aufbau principle and the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: $4\ \text{g}$ of $\text{H}_2$ reacts with $32\ \text{g}$ of $\text{O}_2$ to form water ($2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$). Find the mass of water formed, in grams.
questions.solution:
Moles: $\text{H}_2 = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\ \text{mol}$, $\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{32}{32} = 1\ \text{mol}$.

The equation needs them in the ratio $2 : 1$, and $2 : 1$ is exactly what is supplied — **neither is limiting**, both are used up completely.

$2\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$ gives $2\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$:

mass $= 2 \times 18 = \mathbf{36\ \text{g}}$.

Check by conservation of mass: $4 + 32 = 36\ \text{g}$ ✓

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: Find the total number of orbitals in the shell $n = 3$.
questions.solution:
The number of orbitals in a shell is $n^{2}$.

$n = 3$: $3^{2} = \mathbf{9}$ — made up of one $3s$, three $3p$ and five $3d$ orbitals.

They hold $2n^{2} = 18$ electrons in total.

questions.chapter: Some Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
questions.q: State the postulates of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. Derive an expression for the radius of the $n$th orbit, and explain two limitations of the model.
questions.solution:
**The postulates.**

1. The electron moves in certain **stationary circular orbits** about the nucleus without radiating energy — contradicting classical electrodynamics, and asserted precisely because atoms do not collapse.
2. The angular momentum is **quantised**: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, where $n = 1, 2, 3\ldots$
3. Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron **jumps between** orbits, with $h\nu = E_2 - E_1$.

**Deriving the radius.**

The electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

$mv^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ ... (1)

From the quantisation condition:

$v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}$ ... (2)

Substituting (2) into (1):

$m\left(\dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

$\dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mr^{2}} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

Rearranging for $r$:

$\boxed{r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^{2}}}$

Everything except $n$ is a constant, so

$r_n \propto n^{2}$

Putting in the numbers for $n = 1$ gives the **Bohr radius**, $r_1 = 0.529\ \text{Å}$, and $r_n = 0.529\,n^{2}\ \text{Å}$.

The corresponding energy works out as $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}$, which predicts the hydrogen spectral series exactly — the model's great triumph.

**Two limitations.**

1. **It fails for any atom with more than one electron.** The derivation assumes a single electron feeling only the nucleus. Add a second and the electron-electron repulsion makes the problem unsolvable this way; the model gets helium's spectrum badly wrong.

2. **It contradicts the uncertainty principle.** A Bohr orbit specifies the electron's position **and** its momentum simultaneously and exactly, which $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$ forbids. The orbit is not merely unmeasurable — it is not a meaningful description. This is why quantum mechanics replaced the orbit with the **orbital**, a probability distribution.

Other failures worth knowing: it cannot explain the **fine structure** (the splitting of spectral lines seen at high resolution), the **Zeeman** and **Stark** effects (splitting in magnetic and electric fields), or the **relative intensities** of spectral lines. And the quantisation of angular momentum is simply **asserted**, with no reason given — de Broglie later supplied one by treating the orbit as a standing electron wave, requiring $2\pi r = n\lambda$.
